abstract: Oxygenic photosynthesis relies on the efficient operation of the cytochrome b6f complex (b6f), which acts as the central pacemaker linking linear and cyclic electron transfer chains via its catalytic Q-cycle. Unlike its mitochondrial counterpart, the chloroplast b6f features a unique heme cn/bn pair and an intricate network of conserved water molecules and polar residues near the stromal Qn site, implicated in proton translocation and plastoquinone (PQ) reduction. Here, we investigate the functional significance of the conserved aspartate residue of subunit-IV (PetD:D35), which is located in the centre of the stromal proton resupply channel. Using chloroplast site-directed mutagenesis in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, we generated and characterized three substitution mutants to: glutamate, serine and alanine, to test the contributions of side-chain length, charge, and polarity. Biochemical isolation and EPR spectroscopy revealed that the assembly of the bf and the coordination of the Rieske-ISP subunit remain uncompromised across all isolated b6f variants. However, flash-induced single-turnover kinetics and electrochromic shift measurements demonstrated that the substitution to alanine creates a severe kinetic blockade at the Qn site, trapping low-potential b-hemes in a reduced state and crippling forward electron transfer through the high-potential chain. These findings indicate that PetD:D35 is essential for proton resupply and Q-cycle efficiency, linking stromal Q_n site dynamics to broader redox regulation and photosynthetic viability.
